questions.title: Fever and arm pain after a finger abscess
questions.question: Amir is a 5-year-old boy who presents with a high temperature and pain in his right upper arm for 2 days, worse when he moves the arm. He had an abscess on his right finger 2 weeks ago, treated with oral antibiotics. On examination he has a temperature of 39°C, with redness and swelling over the right upper arm, painful to touch or movement. White cell count and C-reactive protein are raised. What is the most likely causative organism?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Haemophilus influenzae may cause osteomyelitis, particularly in unimmunised children, but it is an uncommon causative organism compared with Staphylococcus aureus.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Mycobacterium tuberculosis may cause osteomyelitis but is an uncommon cause in a setting like this, and presents more insidiously than this acute 2-day history.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Salmonella osteomyelitis has an increased risk specifically in sickle cell anaemia, which is not mentioned here; it is not the typical organism in an otherwise well child.
explanations.D: Correct. Amir most likely has osteomyelitis following haematogenous spread from his recent finger abscess, and the most common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus. Other pathogens include Streptococcus species, and in sickle cell anaemia there is an increased risk of Staphylococcus and Salmonella osteomyelitis specifically.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Most infections are caused by Staphylococcus aureus, with group A Streptococcus as another recognised pathogen; Streptococcus viridans is not the typical organism in paediatric osteomyelitis.

questions.learning_objective: Identify Staphylococcus aureus as the most likely causative organism of paediatric osteomyelitis.

questions.title: Footballer with knee pain and tibial swelling
questions.question: Zain is a 14-year-old boy, a good footballer, who complains of pain in his left knee for a while, worse when he exercises, after training today. On examination there is swelling over the left tibial tuberosity. He is afebrile, with no night pain or pain on waking. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Osteomyelitis would be a very unusual cause here, particularly given the absence of fever, which would be expected in a bone infection.
explanations.B: Correct. This is osteochondritis of the patellar tendon insertion at the knee, often affecting physically active adolescent males (particularly footballers or basketball players). It usually presents with knee pain after exercise, localised tenderness and swelling over the tibial tuberosity, often with hamstring tightness, and is bilateral in 25-50% of cases.
explanations.C: Incorrect. While pain might be referred to the knees from the hips in Perthes disease, this is unlikely to explain localised tibial-tuberosity swelling in this boy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fever is absent, and he can still weight bear and exercise, both of which argue strongly against septic arthritis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis affects the hip, and would not present with swelling over the tibial tuberosity.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise tibial-tuberosity swelling and exercise-related knee pain in a physically active adolescent as Osgood-Schlatter disease.

questions.title: Toddler with a red swollen knee and fever
questions.question: Edward, aged 3 years, woke up complaining of pain in his right leg. He has become more unwell and lethargic, with a temperature of 39°C, heart rate 180/min, respiratory rate 25/min. His right knee is red and swollen, and he cries if it is extended or flexed. There is a small healing insect bite on his right ankle. He has no other medical history. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The arthritis of Henoch-Schönlein purpura would usually be accompanied by its characteristic purpuric rash, and a high fever like this would not be typical.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis does not usually present so acutely, with a single red, swollen joint appearing over hours; it is a more chronic, often multi-joint process.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osteomyelitis is the main differential diagnosis to distinguish from septic arthritis, but the joint itself (rather than the bone) is what is red and swollen here, with pain on movement of the joint pointing to the joint as the primary site.
explanations.D: Correct. Edward has septic arthritis, which needs to be differentiated from osteomyelitis. His knee joint itself is red and swollen with pain on movement, making septic arthritis more likely; an ultrasound and aspiration of the joint should be performed urgently to confirm this and guide treatment.
explanations.E: Incorrect. There is no history of trauma given in this vignette, making a traumatic cause unlikely as the explanation for this acute, febrile, red swollen joint.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise an acutely red, hot, swollen single joint with fever and refusal to move as septic arthritis.

questions.title: Polyarthritis with a salmon-pink rash
questions.question: Karen, aged 5 years, presents with 2 weeks of lethargy, fever and painful wrists and knees. She has a temperature of 38.5°C and a subtle erythematous rash on her trunk. Several joints are swollen, warm and painful, including wrists, right elbow, knees, left ankle and left hip, with cervical lymphadenopathy and a palpable spleen. Blood tests show: Hb 85 g/L, WBC 17×10⁹/L, neutrophils 10.4×10⁹/L, platelets 366×10⁹/L, normal blood film, ESR 70 mm/hour, ANA negative, double-stranded DNA negative, antistreptolysin O titre normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia needs to be considered given the anaemia, but is less likely as Karen has numerous joints affected in an inflammatory pattern and her blood film is normal, without blast cells.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Epstein-Barr virus infection is unlikely as it rarely causes widespread polyarthritis of this pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Post-streptococcal arthritis is unlikely as the antistreptolysin O titre is normal, although a repeat blood test would be needed to confirm the titre remains low over time.
explanations.D: Incorrect. SLE may have similar clinical features but is unlikely as the ANA and double-stranded DNA are both negative; SLE is also very uncommon at this young age.
explanations.E: Correct. Systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the most likely diagnosis, given her systemic illness, polyarthritis (more than four joints) and salmon-pink coloured rash. The raised neutrophil count and markedly raised ESR are consistent with this diagnosis, and the negative ANA/dsDNA/normal ASOT help exclude SLE and post-streptococcal arthritis respectively.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise fever, polyarthritis and a salmon-pink rash with negative autoimmune/streptococcal serology as systemic-onset JIA.

questions.title: Acute limp after a coryzal illness
questions.question: Dominika is a 3-year-old girl who presents with an acute onset limp not present the previous day. She was unwell 2 weeks ago with a coryzal illness. The pain is in her right leg, present only on walking. Her temperature is 37°C, the hip and leg look normal, but passive movement of her right hip shows decreased external rotation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. A bone tumour is rare at this age and would usually present more insidiously, not with this acute-onset limp following a recent viral illness.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Perthes disease usually occurs in slightly older children (aged 5-10 years), rather than a 3-year-old with this acute post-viral presentation.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the most common cause of acute hip pain in children, occurring in those aged 2-12, often following or accompanying a viral infection. Presentation is with sudden onset pain in the hip or a limp; there is no pain at rest, but decreased range of movement, particularly external rotation, as seen here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Septic arthritis can be difficult to differentiate from reactive arthritis, but is far less common, and children with septic arthritis are usually systemically unwell with fever, unlike Dominika's normal temperature.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis is more common in overweight teenage girls, not a 3-year-old with a recent coryzal illness.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish reactive arthritis/transient synovitis from septic arthritis and other causes of acute childhood limp.

questions.title: Newborn with inward-turning feet
questions.question: Huw is a baby who is 24 hours old, born by normal vaginal delivery following a normal pregnancy. The midwife notes the baby's feet look abnormal — turned inwards but of normal size. On passive movement the foot can be manipulated so that it can be fully dorsiflexed to touch the front of the lower leg (the neutral position). What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. This is a common problem caused by intrauterine compression. The foot is of normal size, the deformity is mild, and it can be corrected to the neutral position with passive manipulation, as described here — this passive correctability is the key distinguishing feature from fixed structural deformities.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Talipes calcaneovalgus is a fixed bony deformity, in which the foot is everted and dorsiflexed, not correctable to neutral in the way described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Talipes equinovarus is a fixed bony deformity in which the foot is inverted and supinated; passive movement to a normal, neutral position is not possible, unlike this case.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tarsal coalition is a diagnosis made in adolescent years, not in a newborn.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Vertical talus is seen in children with rocker-bottom feet, who often have other congenital abnormalities, not this passively correctable inward-turned foot.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish positional talipes equinovarus from fixed talipes deformities using passive correctability.

questions.title: Recurrent fractures with blue sclera
questions.question: Harry is an 18-month-old boy brought to the emergency department because he will not weight bear and cries when his left leg is moved. He is afebrile with an otherwise normal examination, except his sclera has a slight blue tinge. An X-ray shows a fracture of his femur, with the bones looking osteoporotic; his mother cannot give a history of trauma. He broke his left arm 4 months ago, similarly unexplained. His older sister, present with them, has her arm in a splint having recently fractured it too. What is the most likely diagnosis for Harry?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Accidental injury is possible in principle, but does not explain the recurrent pattern (a previous unexplained arm fracture) or the blue sclera and similarly affected sibling.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Although non-accidental injury needs to be considered and addressed in parallel, the abnormality of the bones on X-ray (osteoporotic appearance) makes osteogenesis imperfecta more likely; child-protection concerns should be investigated alongside, not instead of, the medical work-up.
explanations.C: Correct. Harry is likely to have osteogenesis imperfecta (type 1). It presents with fractures in early childhood, with osteoporotic-looking bones on X-ray. Children often have blue sclera, though this can be difficult to identify with confidence. The condition is autosomal dominant, and it is likely his older sister Amy has it as well, given her similar unexplained fracture history.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteomyelitis does present with a painful leg, but would usually be associated with fever and redness over the area, and the X-ray would usually be normal at presentation, unlike the osteoporotic bone appearance described here.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osteopetrosis is also an autosomal dominant disease that can present in its milder form with fractures, but the bones look dense (not osteoporotic) on X-ray, which is the opposite of what is described here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise recurrent unexplained fractures, blue sclera and a similarly affected sibling as osteogenesis imperfecta, while addressing NAI concerns in parallel.

questions.title: Toddler with a swollen, held-flexed thigh and fever
questions.question: Emma, aged 3½ years, presents to the Emergency Department with a 24-hour history of a limp and pain in her left thigh, with no history of trauma. Her temperature is 38.9°C and her pulse is 150 beats/min. On examination the left thigh is swollen and held flexed and abducted, and she cries if it is moved. The upper leg is slightly red and warmer to touch than the right leg. Paracetamol has had no effect. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cellulitis would show more diffuse skin erythema without the specific hip-flexed-and-abducted positioning suggestive of joint irritation seen here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no history of trauma, and a fractured femur would not typically present with fever and this positioning suggestive of joint pathology.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osteomyelitis is an important differential, but this presentation, with the joint held flexed and abducted (the position that minimises pressure within an inflamed hip joint) and severe pain on any movement, is more suggestive of an intra-articular process.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Perthes disease usually presents in slightly older children with a more insidious limp, not this acute, febrile, systemically unwell picture with a hot swollen thigh.
explanations.E: Correct. It can be difficult to clinically differentiate between osteomyelitis and septic arthritis, but in this child, the very acute history and flexed-and-abducted position of the thigh at rest suggest septic arthritis. Ultrasound (and diagnostic aspiration), blood cultures and inflammatory markers should be performed and intravenous antibiotics started, without delaying treatment for urgent orthopaedic review.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise septic arthritis's characteristic flexed-abducted hip positioning and acute febrile presentation.

questions.title: Toddler who has suddenly stopped walking
questions.question: The parents of Suliman, aged 18 months, bring him to their GP because he has suddenly stopped walking. He is miserable but apyrexial. His left thigh is swollen with no discoloration and is not warm to touch. He is not moving his left foot, but withdraws it on tickling, which leads him to cry. He is unable to weight bear. He has no other medical problems and is not on any medications. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cellulitis would typically show skin discoloration and warmth over the affected area, both of which are explicitly absent here.
explanations.B: Correct. Suliman most likely has a fractured femur. The absence of fever, discoloration and warmth argues against an infective cause (osteomyelitis or septic arthritis), while sudden refusal to weight bear with a swollen thigh and preserved but painful sensation (withdrawing to tickling) is consistent with an unexplained fracture, which in an immobile toddler with no clear mechanism raises a non-accidental injury concern requiring careful further assessment.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis does not typically present this acutely with sudden refusal to weight bear and no other systemic features.
explanations.D: Incorrect. In osteomyelitis and septic arthritis he would be expected to be unwell with fever, and the left thigh would be warm and discoloured, neither of which is present.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Septic arthritis would also be expected to cause fever, warmth and discoloration over the joint, none of which are described here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise an unexplained femur fracture in a pre-mobile infant, without infection signs, as a non-accidental injury red flag.

questions.title: Swollen knee after gastroenteritis
questions.question: Claire is 5 years old and presents with a swollen knee joint for several days, with mild tenderness but she continues to walk with a slight limp. Her mother reports that 3 weeks ago she had a bout of gastroenteritis with two episodes of bloody diarrhoea and one episode of vomiting, which resolved without treatment. She is afebrile with only mild tenderness on passive movement of both knees and ankles, and some generalised swelling around the knees and ankles. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cellulitis would cause more localised skin erythema and warmth rather than this generalised joint swelling with only mild tenderness.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a possible differential, but the clear temporal link to a preceding gastrointestinal infection 3 weeks earlier, and the mild, afebrile presentation, are more in keeping with reactive arthritis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Osteomyelitis would cause bone rather than joint tenderness, typically with fever, which is absent here.
explanations.D: Correct. Claire has reactive arthritis following an episode of gastroenteritis, likely due to enteric bacteria (for example, Campylobacter), given the bloody diarrhoea. She is afebrile, mildly tender, and still able to walk with only a slight limp — a milder, non-septic picture consistent with reactive arthritis rather than a joint infection.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Septic arthritis would be expected to cause more severe pain, fever, and inability or severe reluctance to weight bear at all, none of which fit this milder, ambulant presentation.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise post-gastroenteritis reactive arthritis as a milder, afebrile, ambulant joint presentation distinct from septic arthritis.

questions.title: Nocturnal bilateral leg pain
questions.question: Milly, a 6-year-old girl, is taken to her GP by her mother as she has started waking up at night complaining that her legs hurt, for about 2 months. She goes off to sleep okay but wakes around midnight crying out, and her mother massages her legs before she settles back to sleep. On examination she looks well, her legs look normal, and she has a full range of movement in all joints, with the rest of her examination normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia can cause limb pain, but would usually be accompanied by other abnormal examination findings (pallor, lymphadenopathy, bruising) or blood test abnormalities, not a wholly normal examination as described here.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chondromalacia patellae causes pain specifically related to patella loading (stairs, sitting-to-standing), not this nocturnal, bilateral, general leg-pain pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Complex regional pain syndrome typically follows a specific trauma and affects one limb with allodynia and colour/temperature change, not this bilateral, symmetrical, entirely normal-examination pattern.
explanations.D: Correct. This condition is poorly understood, but the child has episodes of generalised pain in the lower limbs, which often wake them from sleep. It occurs in preschool- and school-age children, the pain is symmetrical in the lower limbs, is not present at the start of the day, and physical activity is not limited. The physical examination, as here, is entirely normal, and no hypermobility is demonstrated.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osteomyelitis would be expected to cause fever, localised tenderness and an unwell-looking child, none of which are present in this well child with a normal examination.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise bilateral, nocturnal leg pain with a normal daytime examination as growing pains.

questions.title: Severe ankle pain after a ball impact
questions.question: Flora is a 12-year-old girl who presents to the Emergency Department for the third time in 10 days. Her right ankle is extremely painful and she is unable to weight bear, arriving in a wheelchair. Ten days ago a ball landed on her foot while playing netball; it has been getting worse since. An X-ray showed no fracture. On examination she has extreme tenderness over the medial aspect of her foot, even to very light touch with cotton wool. The right foot feels slightly colder than the left, though foot pulses are normal. She refuses to let anyone move the foot. She is systemically well with no fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chondromalacia patellae causes anterior knee pain related to patella loading, not this severe foot pain with allodynia following minor foot trauma.
explanations.B: Correct. Flora is likely to have complex regional pain syndrome, which often presents in a single foot or ankle after minor trauma. In addition to severe pain, there may be hyperaesthesia (increased sensitivity to stimuli), allodynia (pain from a stimulus that would not normally produce pain, as with the cotton wool here), and the affected part may be cool to touch with swelling and mottling, as described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Growing pains are bilateral, nocturnal and occur with an entirely normal examination — this is a unilateral, allodynic, trauma-triggered presentation, which does not fit.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osgood-Schlatter disease causes tibial-tuberosity knee pain related to exercise, not this foot presentation with allodynia and temperature change.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Septic arthritis would be expected to cause fever and systemic illness, and would not typically show a normal X-ray excluding fracture with allodynia to light touch as the dominant feature over 10 days without progression to more obvious joint signs.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise disproportionate pain, allodynia and a cool limb after minor trauma as complex regional pain syndrome.

questions.title: Knee pain on stairs in an adolescent girl
questions.question: Suji, a 14-year-old girl, complains of pain in her knees when walking upstairs. She is otherwise well, free of pain while sitting, but has pain in both knees when asked to stand up from her chair. She has no other medical problems and is not on any medication. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Correct. There is softening of the articular cartilage of the patella. It most often affects adolescent females, causing pain when the patella is tightly apposed to the femoral condyles, as in standing up from sitting or walking up stairs, exactly as described. It is often associated with hypermobility and flat feet, suggesting a biomechanical component to the condition.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Growing pains are bilateral, nocturnal leg pains with an otherwise normal examination, not this specific activity-related (stairs, rising from sitting) anterior knee pain pattern.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypermobility can be an associated finding with chondromalacia patellae, but on its own does not explain this specific pain pattern without further examination findings supporting it as the primary diagnosis here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osgood-Schlatter disease causes localised pain and swelling specifically over the tibial tuberosity, related to exercise, in physically active adolescents, which is a different pattern from this diffuse patellofemoral pain on stairs/sitting-to-standing.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osteochondritis dissecans typically causes more localised joint pain, sometimes with mechanical locking symptoms, rather than this classic patellofemoral loading pattern.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise anterior knee pain worse on stairs/rising from sitting, in an adolescent female, as chondromalacia patellae.

questions.title: Knee swelling worse after football
questions.question: Joseph is a 14-year-old boy who presents to his GP with pain and swelling in his right knee for several weeks, worse after playing football. On examination there is swelling over the tibial tuberosity. He has no other medical problems and has been taking paracetamol when the pain is present. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chondromalacia patellae causes diffuse anterior knee pain related to patella loading, not this specific swelling localised over the tibial tuberosity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Growing pains are bilateral, nocturnal and occur with a normal examination, not this localised, exercise-related, swelling-associated presentation in one knee.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypermobility alone does not explain localised tibial-tuberosity swelling worse after football.
explanations.D: Correct. This is osteochondritis of the patellar tendon insertion at the knee, often affecting adolescent males who are physically active, particularly footballers. It usually presents with knee pain after exercise, localised tenderness, and swelling over the tibial tuberosity, exactly as described here, often with hamstring tightness, and is bilateral in 25-50% of cases.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Septic arthritis would be expected to cause fever and acute systemic illness, not this weeks-long, exercise-related, afebrile pattern.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise exercise-related tibial-tuberosity swelling as Osgood-Schlatter disease.

questions.title: Back pain that wakes a child at night
questions.question: Craig is 5 years old and complains that his back hurts, for about 4 weeks. His mother tried to ignore it, as there was nothing to see and ibuprofen seemed to help, but he has now started waking up at night crying out that his back is sore. He has not had a fever. His father suffers from back pain and is currently off work with it. On examination he is reluctant to move his back, with no obvious spinal tenderness, mild scoliosis, and a normal neurological examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Growing pains classically affect the lower limbs, not the back, and back pain in young children is uncommon enough that it should not be dismissed as a growing-pains variant.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Kyphosis describes an abnormal forward curvature of the spine on examination, not the underlying cause of night-waking back pain described here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Back pain in young children is uncommon, and the presence of red flags (young age, night waking, a 4-week duration) means this should not be assumed to be a normal variant without investigation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Osteomyelitis of the spine would usually present with fever, systemic upset and tenderness over the affected area, none of which are present here.
explanations.E: Correct. Craig may have a benign tumour, an osteoid osteoma, which presents with back pain worse at night. Back pain in young children must be taken seriously, as it is uncommon; red flag features include a young age, waking at night, fever, weight loss and focal neurological signs — several of which (young age, night waking, 4-week duration) are present here, warranting imaging.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise nocturnal back pain in a young child as a red flag warranting investigation for tumour, such as osteoid osteoma.

questions.title: Painless limp with asymmetric skin folds
questions.question: Jack is a 14-month-old boy who has only recently started walking. His mother brings him to the GP as she is concerned he walks with a limp. Examination shows a painless limp of his right leg, asymmetry of the skin folds around his right thigh, and his right hip cannot be fully abducted. He has no other medical history, and was born by elective caesarean section for breech presentation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.B: Developmental dysplasia of the hip — late diagnosis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bow legs is a lower-limb alignment variant, not a cause of asymmetric thigh skin folds and reduced hip abduction.
explanations.B: Correct. Jack has developmental dysplasia of the hip. This is usually identified on one of the routine hip screening checks babies receive (at birth and around 6-8 weeks). He was at increased risk as he was a breech presentation. Occasionally it is not identified, as examination is not 100% sensitive, and late presentation is with a painless limp, exactly as described here, with asymmetric skin folds and reduced abduction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Perthes disease typically presents in slightly older children (5-10 years) with a more insidious painful limp, not this painless limp with asymmetric folds in a 14-month-old.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rickets presents with bowing of the legs and other signs of poor bone mineralisation such as swollen wrists, not asymmetric thigh skin folds and reduced hip abduction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs in older, typically overweight, adolescents, not a 14-month-old infant.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a painless limp with asymmetric thigh skin folds and reduced abduction, post-breech birth, as late-presenting DDH.

questions.title: Bow legs with swollen wrists
questions.question: Zahra is a 4-year-old Asian girl whose mother is concerned about her leg shape. On standing, her knees are very widely spaced with her feet held together. On examination she also has swollen wrist joints. She has no other medical history and is not on any medications. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Bow legs (genu varum) is a common normal variant up to around 3 years of age, but the additional finding of swollen wrist joints in a 4-year-old points away from a simple normal variant.
explanations.B: Correct. This girl has bow legs (genu varum), which would be a common variant of normal up until 3 years of age. The finding of swollen wrists leads to the diagnosis of rickets. She should have blood tests to confirm the diagnosis and be started on vitamin D supplementation, along with dietary advice and advice regarding increasing sunlight exposure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Developmental dysplasia of the hip presents with a limp or reduced hip abduction, not bilateral bow legs with swollen wrists.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Perthes disease presents with hip pain and a limp in slightly older children, not bilateral leg bowing with swollen wrist joints.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis occurs in older, typically overweight, adolescents with hip/knee pain, not this presentation.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish rickets (bow legs plus swollen wrists) from simple normal-variant bow legs.

questions.title: Flat feet in a walking toddler
questions.question: Rachel, a 2-year-old girl, is seen for a developmental check by the health visitor. She is walking on her own but has flat feet while walking. When asked to stand on tiptoes she cannot, but when the health visitor passively extends her big toe an arch is demonstrated. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Developmental dysplasia of the hip presents with a limp or reduced hip abduction, not this bilateral flat-foot appearance with a demonstrable arch on toe extension.
explanations.B: Correct. This is a normal variant of childhood. Toddlers learning to walk usually have flat feet due to flatness of the medial longitudinal arch and the presence of a fat pad, which disappears as the child gets older. An arch can usually be demonstrated on standing on tiptoe, or by passively extending the big toe, as shown here. Rachel is unable to stand on tiptoes not because of a pathological condition, but because children are typically unable to do so at this young age.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Positional talipes equinovarus is a newborn foot deformity correctable to neutral, not this later-presenting flat-foot appearance in a walking toddler.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Rickets would typically show additional findings such as bowed legs and swollen wrists, not isolated flat feet with a demonstrable arch.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A fixed flat foot that cannot demonstrate an arch, often painful, may indicate tarsal coalition and needs orthopaedic opinion — but Rachel's arch is demonstrable, making this an unlikely diagnosis here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise flat feet with a demonstrable arch on tiptoe/big-toe extension as a normal toddler variant.

questions.title: Persistent toe-walking since first steps
questions.question: Alliah is a 2½-year-old girl seen in the paediatric outpatient department because her mother is worried about her walking on tiptoes. She was born by normal vaginal delivery at 37 weeks, started walking at 15 months, never crawled but did bottom shuffle. On examination of her gait she mostly walks and runs on tiptoes, and her mother confirms she has done this since she started walking; however, she can walk on her heels if asked to do so. General examination of her legs shows normal tone and reflexes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Children with mild cerebral palsy can present with toe walking, but an increase in tone would be found on examination, which is explicitly absent here (normal tone and reflexes).
explanations.B: Incorrect. In older boys, Duchenne muscular dystrophy should be excluded when toe-walking persists, but Alliah is a girl with normal tone and reflexes, making this diagnosis unlikely.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Growing pains cause nocturnal leg pain rather than a gait abnormality like toe-walking.
explanations.D: Correct. Toe walking is common in young children and may become persistent, usually from habit. The child can walk normally (on her heels) when asked, as Alliah demonstrates. Bottom-shuffling rather than crawling is also a recognised normal variant of the pre-walking developmental pathway, and with normal tone and reflexes on examination, this fits a benign, idiopathic pattern.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Osteomyelitis would present with pain, fever and localised tenderness, not this painless, voluntary-appearing gait pattern with a normal general examination.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish idiopathic toe-walking from a pathological cause using tone, reflexes and the ability to heel-walk on request.
